regenerable_on: a guest carrying OpenZFS >= 2.3: `zpool status -j` arrived in 2.3, and the lab's Ubuntu 24.04 image ships 2.2.2, which produces no storage payload at all — a drift run there regenerates the network variants and silently skips this one
note:
A file-backed five-wide raidz1, staged in the lab and faulted deliberately, because the failure paths are where the facts that matter live and a healthy capture teaches none of them. Two DIFFERENT injuries, on two different members, so the specimen separates two things a reader conflates: disk3's backing file was overwritten wide and the pool scrubbed, which left checksum errors on that member and nothing else; disk4 was taken OFFLINE, which is what makes the POOL DEGRADED. The pool therefore reads DEGRADED with Errors=0 — parity repaired every one of disk3's bad blocks, so there are no known DATA errors while the per-vdev counter is non-zero. Errors and the counters are different facts, and a reading that treats either as the other is wrong about whether anything was lost.

Kills the hardcoded-healthy port (fleet round a5, fixtures/adversaries/a5_hardcoded_healthy.py): its State is the struct default "ONLINE", its StatusMessage is never read because the pools it was written against had none, its Errors is 0 by initialisation, and UnhealthyVdevs/VdevsWithErrors are stubs returning empty slices. Every one of those is an anchor below, so that subject fails this variant on the facts rather than on its stubbed envelope — which is what the storage/healthy pairing could never establish, since a hardcoded-healthy collector is RIGHT about a healthy pool.

The members are FILES, not disks, and that is visible in the specimen rather than hidden by it: vdev_type is "file", the vdev names are absolute paths, and no leaf resolves to a kernel block device. Every leaf row therefore OMITS Device — the absent channel a nested row has, since a fact value is never null (DESIGN 19) — and no unobservable record claims the resolution could not be done, because it could: devlinks.json is committed, so the alias trees were read and simply hold nothing for a file. Stated bound: this pair cannot TEST that distinction. The could-not-read channel opens only for leaves of type disk, so replaying this variant with devlinks.json deleted emits a byte-identical stream — the payload records what the guest had, and a variant whose members are real disks is what would discriminate.

anchors_note: Written from what the staging DID, before any collector was run over the capture. The pool was created five-wide raidz1 (Redundancy), disk4 was offlined and the raidz group therefore degraded (UnhealthyVdevs holds both, the group and the member — losing the member is what degraded the group), disk3's backing file was overwritten and a scrub left three checksum errors on it and none anywhere else (VdevsWithErrors holds that member alone), zpool answered with its ZFS-8000-9P catalogue prose (StatusMessage, anchored as the exact string, which is the absent-fact assertion inverted: this fact must EXIST), and no data was lost because parity repaired it (Errors=0, beside a non-zero per-vdev counter). Every anchored identifier is the scrubbed spelling, which is what the committed payloads carry: the pool name and the vdev directory are the two operator-chosen words the scrub run was handed.
